items.title: AI-based clinician decision support system for diagnosis of inherited retinal diseases: a multicenter, randomized trial.
items.body: The accurate and timely diagnosis of inherited retinal diseases (IRDs) represents an unmet clinical need in ophthalmology, as the current pathways rely on resource-intensive phenotyping, multidisciplinary expertise and genetic testing. Here we developed Retina4IRD, an artificial intelligence (AI)-based clinician decision support system (CDSS) that predicts 17 genotype categories from retina images. Retina4IRD uses a Vision Transformer model pretrained with RETFound. We then trained and validated Retina4IRD using multimodal data with color fundus photographs and optical coherence tomography scans from 1,843 genetically confirmed patients (3,376 eyes) across China, South Korea and Poland. The top-5 prediction accuracy was 0.904 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.896-0.912) and 0.856 (95% CI: 0.850-0.863) for internal and external validation, respectively. We conducted a randomized controlled trial with 300 participants with suspected IRD randomized 1:1 to either Retina4IRD-assisted specialist arm or specialist-only arm. Of these, 295 participants (median age 33 years, 114 (38.6%) females) with available next-generation sequencing reports were included in the final analysis. The primary outcome was met: top-5 genetic accuracy was significantly higher in the Retina4IRD-assisted specialist arm versus the specialist-only arm (88.5% versus 67.3%, P < 0.001). For secondary endpoints, top-1 to top-4 accuracies all favored the Retina4IRD-assisted specialist arm, with top-1 accuracy of 37.8% versus 22.4% and top-4 accuracy of 81.8% versus 53.1%, respectively. Post hoc analyses demonstrated that, with Retina4IRD assistance, clinicians made better management decisions, and the composite downstream management score indicated significantly higher scores relative to the control group (37.7 versus 28.5, P < 0.001). Our study shows that Retina4IRD is a CDSS tool prior to genetic testing and aligns with clinical workflow for patients with suspected IRDs. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06839170 .
items.why: Retina4IRD, a vision transformer trained on multimodal imaging from 1,843 genetically confirmed patients across three countries, predicts 17 IRD genotype categories and was tested in a 295-patient randomized trial where AI-assisted specialists reached 88.5% top-5 genetic accuracy versus 67.3% for specialists alone. This is a rare combination of external validation and a randomized clinical endpoint with downstream management effects, a template for how diagnostic AI should be evaluated even outside ophthalmology.

items.title: A deep learning model for speech-based prediction of clinical scores in people with Huntington's disease: a longitudinal study with cross-sectional replication.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Sensitive monitoring tools are needed to track progression in neurodegenerative diseases and assess interventions before overt brain damage occurs. We propose speech as a non-invasive, easily collected biomarker to capture disease-related variation over time. We developed and validated Neurodegenerative Disease Speech Network (NDSNet), an automated deep learning model that generates individual speech-derived estimates of contemporaneous clinical scores at each visit in people with Huntington's disease, from presymptomatic stages (Huntington's Disease Integrated Staging System [HD-ISS] stages 0-1) to symptomatic stages (HD-ISS stages 2-3). METHODS: We included data from people with Huntington's disease and healthy controls from three prospective longitudinal studies (Bio-HD, REPAIR-HD, and MIG-HD) with speech recordings and Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale (UHDRS) scores. NDSNet combines a pre-trained wav2vec 2.0 model and a recurrent attentive network in a contrastive learning framework for processing audio waveforms of speech. We trained and cross-validated (10-fold) NDSNet to predict the observed UHDRS scores in people with Huntington's disease across visits, with external validation in a replication cohort (the TPMH study). We then compared NDSNet predictions with striatal atrophy on MRI, the best-established marker of Huntington's disease progression. FINDINGS: Our developmental cohort included 191 people with Huntington's disease and 58 healthy controls, with speech data collected between 2001 and 2025 (MIG-HD data collected in 2001-13 and REPAIR-HD and Bio-HD data collected in 2018-25). The replication cohort included 110 people with Huntington's disease, of whom 78 were not included in the developmental cohort, with speech data collected between Oct 10, 2022, and Feb 5, 2024. In the developmental cohort, we analysed speech recordings obtained from 146 people with Huntington's disease (62 with brain MRI). Relative error between NDSNet predictions and observed clinical scores was 11·4% (95% CI 9·7-12·5) overall. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) between NDSNet-predicted and observed motor scores (ICC 0·87 [95% CI 0·83-0·91]) was similar to that for clinician ratings (ICC 0·847). Predictions showed strong temporal association and responsiveness to observed clinical change at the individual level. Performance remained consistent in 67 people with Huntington's disease in the replication cohort (after excluding 32 participants already included in the developmental cohort; relative error 15·0% [13·0-19·0]; ICC 0·67 [0·38-0·71]). Predicted scores showed MRI associations similar to those of observed clinical scores across symptomatic stages, and stronger associations with striatal atrophy at HD-ISS stages 0-1. INTERPRETATION: NDSNet predictions captured clinically relevant progression from speech in people with Huntington's disease, showed neuroanatomical grounding across disease symptomatic stages, and estimated the subclinical state at HD-ISS stages 0-1. These findings support the use of NDSNet as a scalable tool to complement standard assessments for longitudinal monitoring in Huntington's disease. FUNDING: Neuratris and Centre de Référence Maladies Rares-Maladie de Huntington.
items.why: A deep learning model on speech recordings predicted UHDRS clinical scores in Huntington's disease across four prospective cohorts, with 10-fold cross-validation, external replication in 110 patients, and agreement comparable to clinician ratings plus correspondence with striatal atrophy on MRI. Useful as a template for validating passive digital biomarkers longitudinally, though cohorts are modest in size and the endpoint is a rating scale rather than a hard clinical outcome.

items.title: Natural Cycles Receives Sixth FDA Clearance for AI-Powered Fertility Algorithm
items.body: Birth control and cycle-tracking app Natural Cycles received its sixth FDA clearance for an updated version of its AI-powered NC° Fertility Algorithm. The company previously secured FDA clearances for its birth control app, integrations with Oura Ring and Apple Watch, and over-the-counter availability. The next-generation algorithm combines statistical modeling with machine learning trained on tens of millions of real-world fertility data points… The post Natural Cycles Receives Sixth FDA Clearance for AI-Powered Fertility Algorithm first appeared on .
items.why: Natural Cycles secured its sixth FDA clearance, this time for a next-generation fertility algorithm combining statistical modeling with machine learning trained on tens of millions of real-world cycle data points. This is a regulatory milestone for a cleared algorithmic contraceptive tool that sits squarely in reproductive AI, though the announcement gives no performance data or comparison against the prior algorithm.

items.title: Evaluating large language models for assessment of psychosis risk.
items.body: Psychosis prevention relies on early detection of individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR-P). The effectiveness of the CHR-P state is constrained, in part, due to clinical assessments requiring specialist interpretation of narrative interviews, limiting scalability. Here, we evaluate whether large language models (LLMs; deep learning models trained on large text corpora to process and generate language) can extract clinically meaningful information from such interviews to support psychosis risk assessment. We assessed 11 open-weight LLMs on 678 partial PSYCHS interview transcripts from 373 participants (77.7% CHR-P). Models inferred CHR-P status and estimated severity and frequency across 15 symptom domains, benchmarked against researcher-rated scores. Larger models achieved the strongest classification performance (Llama-3.3-70B: accuracy = 0.80, sensitivity = 0.93, specificity = 0.58). LLM-generated symptom scores showed good correlations with researcher-rated scores (ICC= 0.74, ICC= 0.75). Performance disparities were minimal across most demographic groups but varied across sites. Generated summaries were largely faithful to source transcripts, with low rates of clinically relevant confabulation (3%). Errors primarily reflected over-pathologisation of non-clinical experiences. While accuracy scaled with model size, smaller models achieved competitive performance with substantially lower computational cost. These findings demonstrate that open-weight LLMs have the potential to assess psychosis risk from psychometric interview transcripts, supporting scalable, human-in-the-loop approaches to early detection.
items.why: Eleven open-weight LLMs were benchmarked on 678 clinical high risk for psychosis interview transcripts from 373 participants, with the best model reaching 0.80 accuracy, 0.93 sensitivity, 0.58 specificity, and symptom score ICCs around 0.75 against researcher ratings. Careful evaluation including confabulation rates and site variation, but it is retrospective transcript scoring in a heavily enriched sample, so specificity and real workflow value remain unproven.

items.title: Improving laboratory workforce efficiency using AI-assisted digital cytology within an HPV-based cervical screening programme: A model-based evaluation for the NHS Cervical Screening Programmes.
items.body: OBJECTIVES: We aimed to estimate the time required to review and report cervical cytology slides within a Human Papillomavirus (HPV)-primary cervical cancer screening programme, where cytology is used for triage following a positive HPV test, comparing Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted digital cytology (Genius) with manual microscopy. DESIGN: A decision-tree model of the flow of slides through the National Health Service (NHS) England cervical screening cytology laboratory workflow, parameterised using published evidence and expert input. SETTING: Cytology laboratories within the NHS Cervical Screening Programme in England and Scotland. RESULTS: Screening and reporting 479,125 cytology slides annually in England was estimated to require 31,842 staff hours with AI-assisted digital cytology versus 103,151 hours with manual microscopy. The mean time per slide review and reporting was 4.0 vs 12.9 minutes, respectively, corresponding to a potential 69% increase in overall productivity. CONCLUSIONS: AI-assisted digital cytology can support more resilient cervical screening programmes in the UK and other countries by reducing staff time required for slide review and reporting. These findings may inform policymakers considering strategies to mitigate workforce shortages.
items.why: A decision-tree model parameterised from published data and expert input estimated that AI-assisted digital cytology (Genius) would cut cervical cytology review from 12.9 to 4.0 minutes per slide across the NHS screening programme, a 69% productivity gain. Relevant to anyone thinking about deploying AI in cervical screening at national scale, but it is a workflow model rather than a prospective evaluation, and it reports no accuracy or clinical outcome data.

items.title: An explainable machine learning approach for cervical cancer screening: decoding morphological diagnostic drivers.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Cervical cancer screening in primary care is hindered by expert pathologist shortages and heavy diagnostic workloads, leading to fatigue-induced misdiagnoses. This study evaluated the diagnostic capacity, subpopulation robustness, and operational efficiency of an interpretable machine learning (ML) tool within a large Chinese healthcare network. METHODS: A retrospective database of 5,000 women was audited. Archived liquid-based cytology (LBC) digital slides were evaluated via a parallel validation channel: the LBC-NET pipeline versus a double-blind panel of senior cytopathologists. Diagnostic safety was tested by stratifying data across age, vaginal infections, and menopause conditions. Algorithmic transparency was quantified using game-theoretic Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and morphological feature tracking. Operational efficiency was evaluated via continuous cumulative distribution curves. RESULTS: For detecting high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions or worse (HSIL+), the ML model achieved a clinical sensitivity of 92.5%, significantly outperforming the manual method at 84.2% ( < 0.001), with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.94. Subgroup stratification demonstrated that menopausal tissue atrophy or active vaginal infections caused no significant performance degradation ( > 0.05). SHAP analytics revealed that the nucleus-to-cytoplasmic ratio and nuclear hyperchromasia intensity were the core predictive metrics. Operationally, the ML system compressed the median slide-review time by 63.0%, escalating the daily screening capacity by 175% and reducing specialist referral consultations by 45.2%. CONCLUSION: The interpretable ML tool provides a reliable and fast clinical choice for massive cervical cancer screening.
items.why: A retrospective audit of 5,000 archived liquid-based cytology slides in a Chinese network found the LBC-NET pipeline detected HSIL+ with 92.5% sensitivity versus 84.2% for a blinded senior cytopathologist panel, with stable performance in menopausal and infected subgroups and 63% faster review. The head-to-head comparison against expert readers and subgroup robustness are strengths, but it is retrospective, single-network, and lacks external validation or prospective deployment.

items.title: Perceptions of simulated artificial intelligence in medical consultations: associations with stress, memory, and perceived credibility.
items.body: The growing integration of digital technologies into healthcare requires understanding the impact of different consultation modalities on patient stress, memory and perceived credibility. This study compared different consultation modalities (human physician, in person or via video call; AI-style physician, as a chatbot or avatar) in standardized simulated medical consultations involving the delivery of bad news. For the AI-styled physician consultations, a Wizard of Oz design was used, in which participants were told they interacted with an AI physician while a human controlled the interaction. 163 healthy participants experienced either a human or an AI physician. Stress was measured through ratings and salivary cortisol, alongside memory retrieval and situation credibility. Human-based consultations led to higher stress levels than AI-styled formats. Greater perceived credibility was associated with stronger stress responses. Memory retrieval was lowest in the AI-styled chatbot condition. These findings show that different consultation modalities are associated with varying levels of stress and memory in medical settings. AI-styled physician interactions may reduce stress in routine medical communication, but their use should be carefully considered for critical medical communication.
items.why: In a Wizard of Oz experiment with 163 healthy volunteers receiving simulated bad news, purportedly AI consultations produced lower stress and cortisol than human clinicians, while the chatbot format yielded the worst memory retrieval. An unusual look at how patients respond to AI-delivered communication, though the simulated interaction, healthy participants, and fake AI limit clinical transfer.

items.title: AI-derived oocyte morphology and follicular fluid biomarkers in donors.
items.body: Oocyte quality is a key determinant of reproductive success, yet its assessment in assisted reproduction largely relies on subjective morphological criteria. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based image analysis has introduced greater objectivity into oocyte evaluation; however, the biological features captured by AI-derived morphological scores remain incompletely defined. In this study, we integrated AI-based oocyte morphology with molecular profiling of follicular fluid (FF) to identify biological correlates of oocyte competence. Reproductive outcomes were analysed in 49 young oocyte donors (20-33 years), while FF samples pooled per woman from a subset of 25 donors were analysed for metabolic (glucose, total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL, LDL, APOA1), extracellular matrix-related (HSPG2/Perlecan), signaling-related (Gremlin-1), and fertility-related (AMH, LH, FSH) biomarkers. AI-derived oocyte quality scores were positively associated with specific intrafollicular markers, including glucose, total cholesterol, HDL, AMH, and HSPG2, while no associations were observed with triglycerides, LDL, Gremlin-1, LH, or FSH. APOA1 showed a positive trend with the AI score. These findings provide a biological context for AI-based oocyte morphological assessment by linking digital image-derived scores with metabolic and structural features of the follicular microenvironment. The integration of AI-driven morphology with donor follicular fluid biomarker profiling may contribute to the development of more objective and biologically informed approaches for oocyte quality evaluation in assisted reproduction.
items.why: In 49 young oocyte donors, AI-derived oocyte morphology scores correlated with follicular fluid glucose, cholesterol, HDL, AMH, and HSPG2 but not with triglycerides, LDL, LH, or FSH. It offers a biological interpretation of what AI oocyte scores may capture, which is directly relevant to REI, but the sample is tiny, biomarkers were pooled per woman, and no link to live birth is shown.

items.title: Data-driven endocrine-metabolic phenotypes in young women with polycystic ovary syndrome and associations with cardiometabolic risk markers.
items.body: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a heterogeneous endocrine disorder associated with reproductive dysfunction and increased cardiometabolic risk. Conventional diagnostic phenotypes may not adequately capture endocrine-metabolic variability, particularly in young women. We aimed to identify data-driven endocrine-metabolic phenotypes in young women with PCOS and assess their associations with selected cardiometabolic risk markers. This cross-sectional study included 1032 women aged 16-25 years with PCOS diagnosed according to the Rotterdam criteria, selected from 1300 consecutive patients evaluated at a tertiary gynecological endocrinology center in Poland between 2018 and 2025. Principal component analysis (PCA) followed by Gaussian mixture model clustering was used to identify latent endocrine-metabolic subgroups. Cardiometabolic outcomes included impaired glucose tolerance (2-hour plasma glucose ≥ 140 mg/dL), elevated triglyceride/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (TG/HDL) ratio, elevated non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (≥ 130 mg/dL), and a composite endpoint. PCA retained 10 components explaining 81.9% of total variance. The optimal clustering solution identified two subgroups: a predominant mixed endocrine-metabolic subgroup (n = 954; 92.4%) and a smaller thyroid/autoimmune-enriched subgroup (n = 78; 7.6%) characterized by higher anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels. Cluster assignment certainty within the selected model was high, although sensitivity analyses suggested that the latent structure was partially driven by thyroid/autoimmune-related variables. The thyroid/autoimmune-enriched subgroup showed a higher prevalence of an elevated TG/HDL ratio, whereas differences in glucose tolerance and non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol were less pronounced. These findings suggest the presence of exploratory endocrine-metabolic subgroup structure in young women with PCOS, including a thyroid/autoimmune-enriched subgroup associated with modest differences in lipid-related cardiometabolic risk markers. The observed heterogeneity extends beyond conventional diagnostic classifications, although external validation and longitudinal studies are required to determine clinical relevance and reproducibility. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was not registered as a clinical trial, as it was an observational cross-sectional analysis.
items.why: PCA plus Gaussian mixture clustering in 1032 young women with PCOS produced two subgroups, with a small thyroid/autoimmune-enriched cluster showing modestly higher TG/HDL ratios. The cohort is a decent size and directly relevant to reproductive endocrinology, but the structure is cross-sectional, unvalidated externally, and the authors themselves call it exploratory.

items.title: Performance of Large Language Model-Based Chatbots in Primary Health Care Teleconsultations: A Comparison Between Human and Artificial Intelligence-Generated Responses.
items.body: INTRODUCTION: Telehealth is a strategic component of primary health care and has advanced in Brazil through the National Telehealth Program. Its benefits can be enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI), which has emerged as a promising tool. This study aims to compare the performance of real human and AI-generated responses to queries submitted to the teleconsultation services of the Telehealth Center of the UFMG Faculty of Medicine (NUTEL FM-UFMG), a member of the Telehealth Brazil Program. METHODS: This is a comparative cross-sectional study of 180 real human and AI-generated responses, evaluated in a blinded manner according to quality criteria (medical adequacy, conciseness, coherence, and comprehensibility), risk potential, authorship identification accuracy, and inquiry resolution. Data from NUTEL FM-UFMG (January 2020 to May 2024) were utilized, covering cardiology, endocrinology, and obstetrics/gynecology (OB-GYN). Statistical analysis included the Shapiro-Wilk test, Kruskal-Wallis test, Nemenyi multiple comparison test, chi-square test, and Fisher's exact test. RESULTS: Across all specialties, a significant difference was observed in comprehensibility, with AI mean scores surpassing those of humans. For the remaining quality criteria, as well as for risk potential and inquiry resolution, no significant differences were found, despite AI scoring higher than humans. Within specific specialties, significant differences was observed in endocrinology (except conciseness) and cardiology (in conciseness); AI showed superior means. Across all specialties, as well as individually within endocrinology and OB-GYN, the accuracy of authorship identification (human vs. AI) was statistically significant. CONCLUSION: Despite existing limitations, AI demonstrates substantial potential as a support tool for teleconsultation services.
items.why: Blinded raters compared 180 real teleconsultation answers from Brazilian primary care specialists, including obstetrics and gynecology, against LLM-generated responses and found AI equal or better on most quality criteria and superior on comprehensibility. It is a useful signal for LLM decision support in teleconsultation, but the design is a retrospective text comparison with no patient outcomes and raters could often identify authorship.

scored.title: AI-based techniques in sperm detection.
scored.why: This review summarizes deep learning sperm detection in azoospermia and cryptozoospermia, including augmented reality search aids and AI-microfluidic isolation, with early reports of sperm recovery in samples previously called negative. Highly relevant to REI practice, but it is a narrative review and the underlying clinical validation is still thin.

scored.title: The FDA was all in on AI. Will that change?
scored.why: MedTech Dive reports that senior turnover at the FDA has cast doubt on the pace of the agency's cross-agency AI strategy. Regulatory tempo matters to anyone planning a clinical AI submission, but the piece is thin on specifics and offers no concrete policy change.

scored.title: Characterization and Validation of EHR Computable Phenotypes for Long COVID Using Patient-Reported Symptoms: Insights from the Nationwide RECOVER Program.
scored.why: Using 1,501 RECOVER participants with linked EHR data, the authors trained a computable phenotype for highly symptomatic long COVID validated against patient-reported symptoms, achieving AUROC 0.80 and AUPRC 0.58. Useful for cohort identification and trial recruitment, but modest precision and no external health system validation make this a workmanlike phenotyping paper rather than a practice changer.

scored.title: Large language models for interpretation of health checkup results.
scored.why: Four LLMs were benchmarked on interpreting structured health checkup values from Korean national insurance data, reaching 0.95 accuracy with chain-of-thought prompting while showing weakness on blood pressure categories and sex and age biases in some markers. The bias and threshold findings are mildly instructive, but the task is essentially rule-based lab flagging with no patient outcomes or clinician comparison.

scored.title: Multi-modal Stacking Machine Learning Model for Predicting Lymph Node Metastasis in Cervical Cancer.
scored.why: A stacking ensemble combining habitat radiomics from multiparametric MRI with clinicopathological variables predicted lymph node metastasis in early cervical cancer, reaching AUC 0.875 in an external validation cohort of 125 patients. External validation lifts it above the typical single-center radiomics paper, but it remains retrospective, the external cohort is small, and there is no comparison against radiologist reads or surgical decision impact.

scored.title: Predictive modeling with machine learning for low birth weight in the state of São Paulo: a retrospective population-based study.
scored.why: Logistic regression and random forest were trained on 2.5 million São Paulo live birth records to predict low birth weight, with balanced logistic regression best at AUC 0.850 and sensitivity 0.69. The population scale is real, but predictors include newborn characteristics, there is no external validation or temporal holdout, and simple regression beating the forest suggests limited added value.

scored.title: Evidence integration: The transformative role of artificial intelligence in maternal health.
scored.why: An umbrella review of 34 AMSTAR 2 screened reviews on AI in maternal health found consistent claims of risk prediction for hypertensive disorders, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, and perinatal mental health, but inconsistent external validation, fairness auditing, and prospective evaluation. Useful as a map of the translation gap in maternal health AI, though it is a review of reviews with no primary evidence.

scored.title: Non-contrast MRI Radiomics Nomogram for Predicting Recurrence and Progression-Free Survival in Cervical Cancer following Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy.
scored.why: A non-contrast MRI radiomics plus clinical nomogram stratified progression-free survival after chemoradiotherapy in cervical cancer across two centers, with an external validation set of 31 patients. Avoiding gadolinium is practically appealing, but the validation cohort is too small to establish reliable discrimination or calibration.

scored.title: Reply to the letter to the editor: "Machine learning model for predicting preeclampsia-related adverse outcomes".
scored.why: In an authors' reply, the team reports calibration curves and Brier scores of 0.010 and 0.068 for their gradient-boosted preeclampsia adverse-outcome model in German and North American cohorts, with AUCs of 92% and 87%. The underlying externally validated model is worth knowing about, but this correspondence adds only calibration detail and concedes that head-to-head comparison against the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio and net benefit analysis are still undone.

scored.title: Performance of artificial intelligence in the collection of patient history in general practice.
scored.why: A cross-sectional online study with 204 French general practitioners compared 942 patient histories collected by physicians versus AI, finding AI more complete for allergies, family history, and older patients. The abstract gives almost no detail on which model was used or how completeness was adjudicated, which limits how much weight the conclusion can carry.

scored.source: Eur J Nucl Med Mol Imaging
scored.title: Preoperative PET/CT phenotype of gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma: integrated morphological, metabolic, serological, and explainable machine-learning analysis.
scored.why: In 144 retrospective cervical cancer patients, PET/CT morphology plus tumor markers distinguished gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma by a low-FDG-uptake, infiltrative, CA19-9-positive phenotype, with tree ensembles and SHAP used for interpretation. The phenotype description is clinically interesting for a hard-to-recognize entity, but only 22 GAS cases and no external validation make the models exploratory.

scored.title: Kompass Diagnostics Scales Rapid Finger-Prick Hormone Testing
scored.why: Kompass licensed a University of Chicago silicon biosensor platform to commercialize finger-prick hormone panels, including estradiol, that return results in about ten minutes for IVF and egg freezing monitoring. Point-of-care estradiol could meaningfully change cycle monitoring logistics, but the item reports a licensing deal with no published analytical or clinical performance data.

scored.title: Hertility’s Annual Report Reveals Reproductive Health Knowledge Gaps
scored.why: Hertility analyzed more than 500,000 patient assessments and reports widespread wearable and cycle-tracking use alongside persistent gaps in basic reproductive health knowledge. The dataset size is notable for anyone building patient-facing fertility tools, but this is a self-published company report with no methods or peer review.

scored.title: How Generative AI Should Transform Clinical Decision Support.
scored.why: A JAMA viewpoint arguing for how generative AI should reshape clinical decision support, with no abstract provided. Opinion pieces in high-profile journals can shape framing, but there is no evidence here and nothing actionable for practice.

scored.title: Elevated Circulating AIF1L as a Cell-Free RNA Biomarker of Preeclampsia Impairs Trophoblast Function via Mitochondrial Dysregulation.
scored.why: Multi-omics plus a GLM machine learning step produced a 10-gene cfRNA nomogram for preeclampsia (AUC 0.989) and cell experiments implicated AIF1L in trophoblast mitochondrial function. The AUC is implausibly high for a clinical screening test and the validation is transcriptomic rather than prospective, so treat the diagnostic claim cautiously despite the interesting mechanism.

scored.title: Fusion Gene Detection Enhances Clinical Outcome Prediction of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Through Machine Learning Analyses.
scored.why: Machine learning models combining a 20-gene fusion panel with Milan criteria, AFP, and grade predicted HCC recurrence and 3-year survival with about 72% accuracy in 200 samples. Modest accuracy, small cohort, and a train/test split within one sample set limit confidence, and there is no reproductive relevance to offset that.

scored.title: Machine Learning Analysis of Maternal Mortality Determinants in Nigeria: An Exploratory Study.
scored.why: XGBoost and random forest were applied to 65 years of national-level Nigerian time series data to rank determinants of the maternal mortality ratio, with female tertiary education and service employment ranking highest. Ecological annual data give very few effective observations, so the machine learning adds little beyond descriptive association and cannot support causal or policy claims.

scored.title: Deep Learning for Automated Classification and Dynamic Risk Prediction of Retained Products of Conception on Postpartum Ultrasound.
scored.why: The title describes a deep learning system for classifying retained products of conception on postpartum ultrasound with dynamic risk prediction. No abstract was provided, so design, cohort size, and validation cannot be assessed and the item must be scored conservatively.

scored.title: Explainable AI in Male Infertility: A Clinical Roadmap for Shared Decision-Making.
scored.why: A perspective piece proposing a governance and explainability roadmap for AI in male infertility, covering SHAP, LIME, saliency maps, bias audits, and device regulation. Directly on-beat for reproductive medicine but contains no new data or evaluation.

scored.title: Systems-level genomic analyses reveal shared mechanisms underlying endometriosis and sleep disorders.
scored.why: Combining NHANES cross-sectional analysis, bidirectional Mendelian randomization, and xQTL intersection, the authors report an association between endometriosis and sleep disorders and 37 shared candidate genes. The clinical association rests on wide confidence intervals near the null and the machine learning is a minor prioritization step in a multi-omics pipeline.

scored.source: Zhonghua Fu Chan Ke Za Zhi
scored.title: [Radiomics and deep learning in the prediction of spontaneous preterm birth using cervical ultrasound].
scored.why: A Chinese-language report on radiomics and deep learning applied to cervical ultrasound for predicting spontaneous preterm birth. No abstract is available, so cohort size, design, and validation cannot be judged despite the topic being squarely on-beat.

scored.title: PMOS Linked To Increased Cardiovascular Disease Risk, Study Finds
scored.why: A large records-based study of 413,450 US women reports elevated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome independent of standard risk factors. The cohort is large and clinically important for reproductive endocrinology, but there is no AI or algorithmic component, so it falls outside this digest's scope, and the summary is only a brief news blurb.

scored.title: Doctronic Acquires Summer Health to Expand into Pediatric Primary Care
scored.why: Doctronic acquired Summer Health to extend its AI primary care platform into pediatrics. A small consolidation move with no deal terms, product evidence, or clinical outcomes reported.

scored.title: Smart Toilet Sensor Startup Is Flush with $10M Funding
scored.why: Throne Science raised $10 million Series A for an AI toilet camera tracking gut health, hydration, and urinary function, pitched as an early colorectal cancer detector. Novel sensing modality but the cancer detection claim is aspirational with no validation data presented.

scored.title: Spotting Alzheimer’s Years Earlier Through AI and Clinically Meaningful Insights
scored.why: A contributed piece claims a few minutes of tablet interaction and speech can surface Alzheimer's signals that previously required imaging or years of follow-up. The claim is plausible in principle but the item is promotional commentary without cohort details, validation, or endpoints.

scored.title: What Happens When Patients Trust AI Over Their Doctor?
scored.why: A health law attorney discusses unresolved liability questions when patients bring chatbot advice into the exam room and act on it. Practically relevant to anyone deploying patient-facing AI, but it is a single interview with no case law or data.

scored.title: Candid Health Snags $120M for AI RCM Platform
scored.why: Candid Health raised a $120 million Series D led by Sixth Street Growth for its AI revenue cycle management platform. Large round but administrative rather than clinical, with no performance evidence disclosed.

scored.title: The iPatient Meets the iDoctor.
scored.why: A JAMA commentary piece on the interplay of the digital patient record and AI-driven clinicians, with no abstract or data provided. Nothing in the supplied text supports substantive findings, so it is opinion of unknown depth and low priority.

scored.title: Ferroptosis-associated ALOX12 suppresses ovarian cancer progression through MAPK signaling pathway.
scored.why: Bioinformatics with WGCNA and machine learning flagged ALOX12 as a ferroptosis-related tumor suppressor in ovarian cancer, supported by in vitro and in vivo assays. The AI element is incidental feature selection and there is no clinical validation, so this is basic cancer biology rather than clinical AI.

scored.title: Using artificial intelligence to analyze violence against women in São Paulo.
scored.why: The authors adapted CRISP-DM into a health research framework and applied time series and geospatial analysis to 80,148 reports of violence against women in São Paulo, projecting continued increases. This is descriptive surveillance with light modeling and a proposed process framework, with little that changes clinical or research practice.

scored.title: Identification and importance analysis of osteoporosis risk factors in perimenopausal women based on the Transformer-LSTM hybrid model and SMOTE.
scored.why: A single-center retrospective dataset from one Beijing gynecology department was used to train a Transformer-LSTM classifier for osteoporosis in perimenopausal women, with SMOTE oversampling and reported AUC around 0.92. There is no external validation and applying SMOTE before evaluation typically inflates minority-class metrics, so the performance claims should not be taken at face value.

scored.title: A prognostic immune signaling-related lncRNA-circRNA-mRNA network model for cervical cancer using machine learning.
scored.why: Public transcriptomic data were used to build a circRNA-lncRNA-mRNA immune network and a LASSO prognostic model for cervical cancer, with test AUC 0.89 and docking-based support for a miR-210:DLEU1:ITPR1 axis. Purely in silico with bootstrap internal validation only, so it is hypothesis-generating bioinformatics rather than clinically usable.

scored.title: An integrated deep learning and Bayesian computational method-based quantification of angiogenesis in the chick embryo model.
scored.why: The authors built a deep learning plus Bayesian Gompertz pipeline to quantify vessel growth in the chick yolk sac membrane angiogenesis assay, validated pharmacologically with VEGF, anti-VEGF, and hydrocortisone. This is a preclinical image-analysis tool with no clinical endpoint and only tangential connection to reproductive medicine.

scored.title: Bonafide Survey Highlights Perimenopause Mental Health Toll
scored.why: Bonafide's sixth annual survey of over 2,000 symptomatic women aged 40 to 64 reports that anxiety, depression, and panic attacks are the most disruptive perimenopausal symptoms. This is company-sponsored survey marketing with no AI component and no clinical evaluation, so it carries little weight for this reader.

scored.title: TD Bank Group Donates $1M to Advance Menopause Brain Health Research
scored.why: TD Bank donated $1 million to Sinai Health Foundation to expand a study of menopausal hormone therapy for migraines and cognitive symptoms. It is a philanthropic gift with no AI element and no results yet, so it is background noise rather than actionable news.

scored.title: Menstrual Health Startup DITTO Secures $6M To Expand Research Platform
scored.why: DITTO raised $6 million in seed funding for a menstrual health research platform and a multi-nutrient PMS and PMDD supplement. Early-stage funding for a supplement product with no algorithmic component and no efficacy data behind it.

scored.title: Elle, MD Raises C$1.1M to Advance Non-Hormonal Birth Control Ring
scored.why: Elle, MD raised C$1.1 million in pre-seed money to fund human studies of a copper-based non-hormonal vaginal contraceptive ring. Reproductively relevant but pre-clinical, tiny in scale, and with no AI or data component at all.

scored.title: The Code Gets You Paid — The Variant Gets You Treated
scored.why: An opinion piece argues that healthcare AI trained on billing codes misses the genomic detail clinicians actually need to treat patients. The framing is reasonable but it is commentary with no data or specific system evaluated.

scored.title: How AI Inside Clinical Workflows Is Unlocking Patient Throughput
scored.why: An opinion piece argues clinical AI only helps when embedded at the decision point in existing workflows. Familiar implementation advice with no data or deployment results behind it.

scored.title: AI Will Reshape the Patient Experience
scored.why: A commentary predicts AI tools will move from advising patients to taking actions on their behalf. Speculative opinion with no product, study, or evidence attached.

scored.title: Use of heart rate variability in prediction of clinical deterioration in critically ill hospitalised adults: a systematic review protocol.
scored.why: This is a protocol for a systematic review of heart rate variability as a predictor of deterioration in critically ill adults, with no results yet. No AI component, no findings, and no reproductive relevance, so it offers nothing actionable.

scored.title: Mechanistic advances in nanomedicine, nucleic acid therapies, and AI-driven research on cervical cancer.
scored.why: This is a narrative review of nanocarriers, nucleic acid therapeutics, and AI-assisted formulation design in cervical cancer. No new data and the AI content is a brief speculative section, so there is nothing actionable here.

scored.title: Model-Guided Optimization of a Low-Serum Medium for Madin-Darby Canine Kidney Cells Using a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network and Bayesian Optimization.
scored.why: Design of experiments was combined with a Kolmogorov-Arnold network and Bayesian optimization to formulate a 2% serum medium for MDCK cells used in influenza vaccine production. This is bioprocess optimization with no clinical or reproductive relevance for this reader.

scored.title: AI Readiness Starts with Solving Healthcare’s Data Fragmentation Problem
scored.why: A sponsored webinar recap in which health plan panelists discuss resolving data fragmentation before adopting AI. Vendor-sponsored content with no findings of any kind.

scored.title: Silkworm synthetic biology: Toolkit development, chassis engineering, and biomanufacturing applications.
scored.why: A review of silkworm synthetic biology tools, chassis engineering, and silk-based biomanufacturing, mentioning AI-assisted design only in passing as a future direction. Entirely off-topic for this reader with no clinical or reproductive medicine content.

scored.title: AI-redesigned starting points and outcomes enhance protein evolution.
